This dish is a poem to autumn, filled with sweet
sampled:
, fresh flavors of tomatoes, basil and lemon, and topped off with a simple, yet impressive, ravioli crust.

Ingredients

4 cups water

1 1/2 teaspoons salt

3 cups eggplant cut into a 1/2-inch dice

3 cups zucchini, cut into a 1/2-inch dice

3 cloves garlic, minced

3 cups spaghetti sauce

1 1/2 cups breadcrumbs

3 cups parmesan

4 eggs

1 1/2 cups ricotta

2 cups grated mozzarella

Instructions

Add the water, salt, eggplant and zucchini to a large pot, and bring to a boil. Add the garlic, and continue boiling, covered for 12 minutes, or until the vegetables are tender. Remove the pot from the heat and add the spaghetti sauce, breadcrumbs and parmesan. Gradually add the eggs, stirring until smooth. Continue stirring for 3-4 minutes or until the eggs are just set. Add the ricotta and mozzarella, and pour into a lightly greased 13x9-inch glass or ceramic baking dish.

Bake for 30 minutes or until the cheese is melted and the sauce is bubbling. Remove from oven and sprinkle with basil and sliced lemon. Serve hot. Serves 8.

sampled:

Fox, based in Century City, is spending $6 million on a two-year lease. The studio has the option of extending the lease by an additional two years.
A handful of other major studios also have offices in Palm Beach County, including Paramount, Columbia, and Universal.
The move is a coup for Riviera, which is owned by Palm Beach developer William Zabka, and is being billed as the first studio built specifically for film and television production in North America.
Dolph Lundgren, who is starring in Speed II and is a Palm Beach native, is a client of Zabka’s and is a driving force behind the use of the Riviera facility for production.
“The film and TV business is a major focus for Riviera Studios because of its ability to attract film and television production,” Zabka said. “Filming studios such as this are hard to come by, and we welcome the opportunity to bring them to Palm Beach County.”
In addition to movies, the Riviera facility is frequently rented by television production companies.
Last year, Fox and Paramount filmed at the Riviera facility for an undisclosed movie.

The signing is
sampled:

Those two entities are not the same,” De Cambra told The Denver Post. “A law enforcement body camera video would be retained as evidence for 30 days and an arrest or search video would not be retained as evidence for more than 60 days.”

original: Readers may be familiar with the fundamental changes that took place in the Roman world as it converted from paganism to Christianity in the fourth century, and as its emperors sought to govern, through the turbulent times of the fifth to seventh centuries, as
sampled:
the new state Church. But what about the early centuries of the Church’s existence?

This is the period, from the early centuries of the first century to the early fourth, that Christian tradition calls the “dark age” of ancient Christianity. The Church’s first martyrs and leaders, and the first Christian communities, were all wiped out or forced to flee the Roman empire; those that remained in Rome were persecuted by the emperor, and subjected to cultural and religious repression during the early fourth-century persecutions. There is little reliable information about the lives of people during this period.

One exception is a small community called the Laodiceans, who lived on the southern coast of Asia Minor, near what is now Istanbul, and who were perhaps the most famous small-scale early Church community, and the first Christian community to be persecuted by the emperor. The only surviving ancient texts about the Laodiceans are letters that they wrote, and that are now known to have been written by someone who is thought to have been a Laodicean leader. These letters have been studied extensively; what has not been fully appreciated, however, is how the Laodicean community dealt with the challenges that they faced at the time. They have now been translated into English for the first time.

By W. James Antle III

Is Mr. Gorbachev Turning Tail?

Just who is Mikhail Gorbachev? The reformer whose unconventional thinking encourages the Soviet Union to transform itself, or a pushover for reac tionaries who want him to arrogate unlimited power?

By W. James Antle III

Published: July 22, 1991

Mikhail S. Gorbachev's first 100 days as president of the Soviet Union, and as the new chairman of the Soviet Union, were marked by an historic transition of power that left many Americans looking for more. But they should not expect to see many dramatic changes in the Soviet Union for at least another 100, because Mr. Gorbachev is a man of pragmatism, not idealism.

Mr. Gorbachev's first 100 days were spent trying to establish himself as a leader of national strength and unity. There was nothing to be gained by trying to implement immediate reforms, and he knew that. And there is nothing to be gained by trying to reverse them now, as some on the hard-liners are demanding.

Indeed, to the extent that Mr. Gorbachev is a man of idealism at all, it is in his recognition of how the Soviet Union works. While it may have been fashionable among the political gladiators in Moscow to talk about the Soviet Union as a monolithic structure, that is far from the case.

Companies would have to make the disclosures within two weeks of their annual shareholder meeting. The final rule would take effect next year.

original: In the age of Instagram, food is no longer designed to just be food. It’s a set piece, a lifestyle statement of fantastical hyperbole. So we drink unicorn lattes, eat rainbow bagels, and lick our charcoal-
sampled:
infused bacon off tweezers. But have you ever wondered if these culinary obsessions are merely designed to make the people who eat them feel better?

We’re talking about the new breed of health-conscious foodies who are obsessed with eating well, but with zero regard for the health of their bodies. The term “healthy” often means the absence of disease, but not the absence of other things. Eating healthy doesn’t mean your body has enough nutrients to function properly. It also doesn’t mean your body has enough nutrients to keep you from starving. And it most certainly doesn’t mean your body has enough nutrients to give you a life worth living.

This week on Hidden Brain, we’re going to talk about the health obsession with clean eating and whether the health benefits that people claim actually matter. You’ll hear from the author of The Clean 20 and a man recovering from eating disorder, and we’ll discuss the new food fads and whether they’re causing us to make the most basic health and environmental mistakes. Finally, we’ll discuss the new diet trend of “raw celery juice,” which is a real thing that people do.

Hidden Brain is hosted by Shankar Vedantam and produced by Jennifer Schmidt, Parth Shah, Rhaina Cohen, Thomas Lu, and Camila Vargas-Walker. Our supervising producer is Tara Boyle.

The controversial $3 billion corporate tax initiative Measure 97 went down in defeat, according to partial election returns Tuesday night.
Measure 97 was failing 58 percent to 42 percent as of 9:50 p.m.
The defeat follows a hard-f
sampled:
ought campaign waged by a group of local companies, and unionized workers, that argued the initiative would level the playing field between the largest multinational corporations and smaller businesses by closing loopholes and requiring companies to pay taxes on their profits and not just their wages.
The measure would have also increased the state's corporate income tax by 1 percent for seven years.
The measure fell short of the 60 percent vote it needed to pass.
Last week, Washington Gov. Jay Inslee said he would pull his endorsement from the measure, and that of other top state Democrats.
Backed by Amazon, Microsoft and Starbucks and organized by a group of local companies, including Amazon, Alaska Airlines, Expedia, Costco and McDonald's, the effort was largely funded by large corporations.
The measure drew considerable support nationally from the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees Council 31, as well as the Service Employees International Union Local 775.
"This is a historic moment for workers in Washington state, and we are humbled by the opportunity to have brought our fight to this state. The message is clear – no one is above the rules," said RWDSU President Mark Takano.
Backers said the measure would have raised hundreds of millions of dollars a year in taxes that could be spent on education, childcare and public services.
Opponents said the measure represented a tax increase that would have stifled job creation and economic growth in the state.
-- Gordon R. Friedman
